To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) genetic defects affecting subunits within a protein complex manifest by partially-overlapping phenotypes, and (2) disease resulting from mutations in a protein complex can generate a wide range phenotypic presentations.
genetic mutations affecting the expression of a complex subunit generate divergent phenotypes and that the phenotypic presentation may be dependent on the dosage of the mutated gene.

1) mutations in the genes for subunits of the BLOC-2 complex generate divergent phenotypes, 2) the phenotypes of mice with one copy of a BLOC-2 gene deleted are distinct from those with two copies deleted, and 3) the phenotypes are distinct for mice lacking different subunits of BLOC-2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
elucidating the molecular basis of neurodevelopmental disease.
the genetic basis of schizophrenia and other neurodevelopmental disorders and the role of protein complexes in the etiology of these disorders.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathophysiology of schizophrenia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the phenotypic effects of mutations in genes encoding subunits of the same complex are not always identical and may be influenced by the specific subunits affected and the number of copies remaining.
mutations in the genes for BLOC-1 protein complex subunits generate divergent and dosage-dependent phenotypes.
the phenotypes resulting from the disruption of the genes that encode the BLOC-2 and BLOC-1 complexes are different.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic defects in BLOC-1 components have divergent and dosage-dependent phenotypes.
genetic defects affecting subunits in a protein complex manifest by partially-overlapping clinical features.
genetic defects affecting the expression of subunits of a protein complex may generate divergent phenotypes, even when they affect the same cellular pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the loss of one or two alleles of genes encoding subunits of protein-complexes generates different phenotypes in mice, suggesting that the genetic disruption or loss of function of a protein complex generates a wide spectrum of phenotypes in mammals, including humans.
genetic defects affecting subunits within protein complexes can generate divergent phenotypes, even when the subunits are members of the same complex.

the genetic disruption or elimination of different subunits in protein complexes generates a wide range of clinical features, which can be explained by the fact that each protein complex subunit has a different role in the cell.
